t: Absolute monarchy placed the making of law, its execution and the final judgement of cases in one hereditary ruler, justified in early modern Europe by the divine right of kings.
Rulers such as Louis XIV, Peter the Great and Frederick the Great built standing armies, bureaucracies and court cultures that laid foundations of the modern state.
Revolutions between 1688 and 1917 ended absolutism across most of Europe; historians still debate how absolute these monarchs really were, and a few states keep the form today.
dyk: Denmark–Norway’s King’s Law of 1665, the first written constitution in Europe to establish absolute monarchy, declared the king “the most perfect and supreme person on the Earth”, standing “above all human laws”.
ev: Jean Bodin’s Six Books of the Commonwealth defines sovereignty as absolute and perpetual power
Louis XIV begins his personal rule of France on the death of Cardinal Jules Mazarin
Frederick III of Denmark signs the King’s Law, Europe’s first written constitution of absolute monarchy
The Glorious Revolution deposes James II and ends moves towards absolute monarchy in England
Joseph II grants religious toleration and abolishes personal serfdom in the Bohemian lands
The French Revolution begins, and the National Assembly ends absolute monarchy in France
Revolutions sweep Europe; Denmark gives up absolutism and Prussia receives a constitution
Nicholas II’s October Manifesto promises Russia an elected Duma, ending unlimited autocracy

f.power: The monarch alone, as supreme lawgiver, judge and commander, governing through ministers, councils and officials who serve at the ruler’s pleasure
f.legitimacy: Hereditary right sanctified by religion: in early modern Europe the divine right of kings, by which the ruler answered to God alone; elsewhere such sanctions as the Mandate of Heaven
f.chosen: By hereditary succession within a dynasty, usually by primogeniture; a monarch left the throne only by death, abdication, deposition or revolution
f.examples: Kingdom of France under Louis XIV, Denmark–Norway under the King’s Law of 1665, Russian Empire under Peter the Great, Kingdom of Prussia under Frederick the Great, Habsburg Monarchy under Joseph II
